subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My recollection was
bad in that respect; I am sorry. I should have known that a promise might not be fulfilled.
Sugar coming, as it does, from the sterling area, the question of foreign exchange is not involved. Of such taxes as that on sugar the United States Secretary of the Treasury, Mr. Morgenthau, said in his press conference of April 29 last:
The time may come, but not this year, when taxes on food may be necessary; but for the present I am opposed to this kind of tax one hundred per cent. A tax on the poor man's table goes against everything this administration has worked for and stood for.
On the same ground we are unalterably opposed to the sugar tax, and particularly to doubling it now.
The tax on gasoline can be justified only in so far as it applies to pleasure cars. To tax gasoline used for industrial purposes will increase the cost of living. It is another hidden tax which will enter into the prices paid by the consumer and by the poor. Exemption from this tax should certainly be given to the primary industries, and more particularly those of farming and fishing. To-day gasoline enters largely into the cost of agricultural production, and fishermen's operations on both coasts now depend largely upon the gasoline engine and, therefore, upon gasoline. Both these classes of producers are at present in a particularly bad way, and a tax of three cents a gallon on the fuel will further increase the difficulty of these depressed industries.
The hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) said that in several of the provinces, where gasoline is already taxed, specially coloured gasolines are available to farmers and fishermen for their operations. This fuel is tax-exempt. This principle should be carried into the new federal tax. That, I think, is easily undertaken. Particularly in the prairie provinces our people are used to the tax-exempt purple gasoline, and I am sure that the steps which have been taken to ensure that there shall be no abuses have prevented abuses; as a matter of fact, our people have never desired to take advantage of the purple gasoline for anything but its legitimate use.
Much the same criticism must be made of the transportation tax. Most people travel
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell

by bus, train or steamer because they must do so; people, for example, who do not own automobiles must travel by these methods. Business men and commercial travellers will merely charge the added cost in their expense accounts, and the amount will be added to the prices of their products. For them it will not, in many instances, mean much. Again, those who must travel in search of employment or from necessity, soldiers on leave, artisans moving from one place to another to take employment in war industries, will be unable to pass the tax on; hence it will be burdensome and inequitable. If a tax is to be placed on transportation, let it be placed on chair cars, drawing-room and other forms of luxury travel, but not on ordinary tickets.
The special tax on lower priced automobiles is to be increased from 20 to 25 per cent. We have been told many times that the object of the tax is to cut down the purchase of cars in war time, as well as to give some revenue. Obviously the tax has not achieved the first objective, for January, February and March this year made high records for automobile sales. Since this is coupled with the rationing of imported cars, it gives added protection to the highly protected Canadian automobile industry, or rather additional protection and profits to Canadian factories of certain United States corporations. We must cut down the manufacture of private cars; therefore let us do so by means of a priority system, which is the only fair method of approach. Indeed, if we are to fulfil our part in a total commonwealth war effort, there should be neither steel nor rubber nor machine tools nor labour for the building of any but the essential machines of war and the necessities of life. Britain cries aloud for mechanized war equipment; yet we continue to use material and labour in the manufacture of commodities we could do without. North America's role in this war must still be the provision of equipment in larger and larger quantities. The Right Hon. Winston Churchill, Prime Minister of Great Britain, said in a recent broadcast: "Give us the tools and we will finish the job".
In Canada we have not utilized either labour or machinery in the most efficient way. In Great Britain they have planned to diffuse their industrial effort over the whole country. To some extent this is done because they wish to escape the devastating air raids on concentrated industry, but why can we not do something of the same sort for different reasons? Western Canada, for example, with which I happen to be most familiar, has thousands of skilled mechanics who operate local and often small machine shops equipped with lathes, welding apparatus and so forth. Why cannot these men and their skill and 
machines be used to make parts for assembly into machines of war? In my opinion we have a vast reservoir of potential production which is idle at the present time. Such a plan, now in operation in Great Britain, and being considered to some extent in the United States, would not only utilize idle men and machines but prevent the breaking up of established 'homes through the concentration of industry in the large centres. It would do much to prevent congested housing conditions and to keep small communities in being. We must not depopulate the countryside and aggravate the housing situation in our cities, as well as invite still greater post-war problems that we shall have to face. In any event, our post-war problems will be very grave, especially in the industrial centres and around the new war industries.
In connection with the 'housing situation, we regard it as most unfortunate that the budget imposes the sales tax on building materials. By all means forbid the building of luxury homes, but let us do nothing to discourage the building of homes for our people. I do not propose to say much about this feature to-day, because one of my colleagues intends to deal with it more fully in the debate.
In the long run a healthy population is our best defence against aggression, both from within and from without. Health cannot be maintained under housing conditions such as exist in some of our cities, notably Halifax where many of our men of necessity must go at this time. The Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) made a rather bitter attack on this group because before the war we criticized defence estimates; because we were suspicious, and admitted it, of the people who were in charge of our international policy, as a result of not being told what international policy the government was following. But let me tell the minister that year after year, as premier of Nova Scotia, he sat within a few blocks of some of the vilest conditions in Canada, and allowed men, women and children to decay under his very eyes when he had the power at least-which we never had-to eliminate conditions which destroyed the human material upon which ultimately this country must rely in war and in peace. To my mind the building of homes should not be discouraged and the sales tax should not be imposed on building materials. If we are looking for minor sources of revenue I would suggest that the tax on whisky and other spirituous liquors could be further explored. It is argued that an increase would curtail consumption and thus lower our tax receipts

The War-Sinking of Ship
from that source. Well, we can curtail consumption of hard liquor to advantage at any time, so whatever the result, a higher tax on spirituous liquors would at least be a social gain.
In spite, however, of all these facts and criticisms, I realize that the Minister of Finance has tried to be fair within the limits of the economic environment which must determine his financial policy. The staggering conclusion is that within the limits of the present economic system a pay-as-you-go policy is not possible. After we have imposed relatively higher direct and indirect taxes, we shall have to borrow about a billion dollars, or find that amount in some other way, which may entail still further reductions in our standards of living. Under the profit or capitalist system there is no escape from this dilemma. The minister himself virtually stated this in so many words when he said that 'licences would be required for the erection or extension of buildings for industrial or commercial use, or for the installation of new machinery, and so forth. I quote the minister's own words:
This policy of controlling investment will have the important effect of providing a large market for government bonds, but it will have other important effects as well.
Thus war forces us to do what we would not consider doing to meet our many peacetime needs. Indeed, more and more the government which resisted all suggestions for economic and social planning is being forced to undertake it piecemeal, without a comprehensive plan and, therefore, without the effectiveness that it ought to have.
If this war has taught us anything, surely it has taught us that the democracies must learn to plan without regimentation. In the past we have mistaken industrial anarchy for freedom. The aim of this group is to replace the present competitive profit and capitalist system, with its inherent injustices, inhumanity and social and economic anarchy, with a social order in which economic planning will supersede unregulated private enterprise and competition, and in which genuine democratic self-government will be possible; for again let me say that there can be no real democracy and no real democratic selfgovernment until political democracy is rounded out by economic democracy. With our present equipment, and in this scientific age, we should be able to make men and women really free. Only the institution of such a system as is now being generally visualized, not by a few idealists here and there throughout the world but by great masses of thinking men and women, some of whom occupy dominant positions in our own
commonwealth of nations, would bring about the equality of sacrifice that ought to be attainable. Only in a cooperative, planned society would an all-out war effort, with a pay-as-you-go policy, become possible. We should be able to organize our effort on a realistic basis and say that so many units of labour, equipment and materials shall be used for war production, and so many for the production of those things necessary for the welfare of our people. We would then proceed to produce, without profit to monopolies, without interest to bondholders, without mortgaging our country and its future.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SINKING OF VESSEL AND LOSS OF CANADIAN MILITARY PERSONNEL

speakeroldname: Hon. ANGUS MACDONALD (Minister of National Defence for Naval Services):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF SINKING OF VESSEL AND LOSS OF CANADIAN MILITARY PERSONNEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have an announcement to make to the house. I regret deeply that I should have to make it and that it should have to be in such terse form, but this is the form in which the British Admiralty desires that it should be made. The announcement, as authorized by the Admiralty is as follows:
Information has been received that a ship which included among its passengers a party of military personnel has been sunk. It is feared that among those lost are seventy-five military personnel. The next of kin of casualties have already been informed.
I may add that the next of kin of those who have been reported safe also have been informed by the Department of National Defence. I have only to add my own great personal regret at this loss. I am sure every member of this house shares that regret with me, and would like to have the relatives of those who have been lost realize how deeply the sympathy of this house goes out to them in this hour.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on rising to resume the debate after the dinner recess, before which the Minister of National Defence for Naval Affairs (Mr. Macdonald) made an
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell

announcement of losses in the battle of the Atlantic, may I on behalf of our group-and I am sure I speak for members on all sides
of the house-express to the government our sorrow at the loss of more servants of the nation, and to those who have lost relatives, our deepest sympathy in their bereavement.
In my concluding remarks I was outlining what I considered to be the kind of organized society which we should be visualizing, both for the conduct of the war and in preparation for the peace that will follow. In such a social order individuality will not be crushed by a system of regimentation. What we seek is a proper collective organization of [DOT]our economic resources so that we may use them during this war to defeat aggression and afterwards continue to use them to enrich the individual lives of our people. This, in our opinion, summarizes the war and peace aims which our people need to have placed before them in order to secure their maximum effort in the struggle in which we are now engaged. We must show them that in every way Canada fights, not for an old way of life but for a newer, better, freer, more secure and just way of life.
It has been said that in some parts of the country there is a lack of enthusiasm for our war effort. If that is so, it is, I believe, not because the people do no wish to defeat the aggressor nations and all that they stand for, but because the issues have not been placed before the people in a sufficiently striking manner. When I say "the issues", I am thinking, not of the immediate issue of victory or defeat but rather of a much wider issue. For the past few generations we have been progressing toward a form of society different from any which we have ever known. This form of society has been evolving under our very eyes, and in my opinion our people should be encouraged to believe that this evolution will be deliberately speeded up by intelligent and conscious direction.
Some day we hope that most of our young men in uniform will return to us again; some day the men now engaged in our industries will finish their war-time tasks. These men will naturally wish to know what is to follow when peace comes. I have no doubt that ultimately the cause of freedom will triumph. Throughout all history, although freedom may have been trodden under foot for a time, it has inevitably risen victorious in the end. I have no fear that that also will be the outcome of the present struggle. But when it is over, there must not be and, if I read the desire of our people aright, there will not be another lost generation. In the lifetime of most of us in this chamber there has been, not one lost generation, but two. We lost

the flower of one generation in the great war, and another generation was wasted in the depression that followed.
I believe that the youth of our land, called upon to-day to make such heavy sacrifices, expect that this parliament, this representative body, this democratic institution, will now begin to prepare for the time when they will return. I repeat that we ought to be preparing now for the future. While we are calling upon the people of Canada to make the sacrifices outlined in the budget now under discussion; while we are asking our young .men to take their part in this struggle for human freedom, we ought to be making preparations for a fuller, better, more secure, and more democratic way of life. Therefore I wish to conclude with that thought, and to repeat what I have said in this house on former occasions. In my opinion we have been negligent in our duty because we have not yet fully established in this dominion a committee widely representative of labour, agriculture and industry to consider the preparations which we Should be making for the period that will follow this war.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to join with the Minister of National Defence for Naval Affairs (Mr. Macdonald) in expressing our deep sense of loss in the disaster which befell one of our ships, with the consequent loss of a number of our Canadian boys, the announcement of which was made by the minister before the house rose at six o'clock. In expressing our sorrow to the bereaved parents and relatives, I trust that there will be brought home to every one the fact that any financial sacrifices which we may be called upon to make cannot equal the sacrifices of those who have given their lives for their country.
Before I deal with the budget, perhaps the house will bear with me for a moment or two while I refer to an incident which took place on Saturday last and which was ol significant importance to one of the overrun countries of Europe which is still our gallant ally. I refer to Poland, whose people commemorated on Saturday, May 3, the one hundred and fiftieth anniversary of that country's constitution. It was on May 3, 1791, that the Polish diet adopted a new constitution which changed the political organization of that country and achieved great reforms on behalf of her people. It has been affirmed by some historians that the constitution set up in that year, and brought about without the shedding of blood, was one of the greatest events of the century I feel

THhe Budget-Mr. Reid
sure that members of the House of Commons will welcome an opportunity of tendering to the Polish consul and the stricken people of Poland our sympathy and felicitations upon their memorable anniversary, with the assurance that the people of Canada look forward with the utmost confidence to the day when the conqueror shall be banished from their land.
With regard to the budget, my first words are to commend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) for his splendid presentation on Tuesday last. The minister's manner of delivery on that occasion left no doubt as to his absolute confidence in the willingness of the Canadian people to accept whatever burdens may be necessary. From the consensus of opinion which has been expressed throughout the country since the budget was brought down, this confidence would seem to be fully justified. The financing of our war expenditures, coupled with the difficulties of helping to finance Great Britain's purchases and the further difficulties in connection with payments to the United States, is a task of considerable magnitude. This is especially so when it is realized that we are endeavouring to cope with these new conditions by using the now out-dated methods which were used during the days when we operated under the gold system-a system which, by the way, only a few short years ago was pronounced by kings, prime ministers and financial experts alike in almost every country in the world as the alpha and omega of our very existence on this earth. How foolish it all sounds now when one remembers a speech made in 1930 by the then prime minister of Great Britain, the late Right Hon. Ramsay MacDonald, when he said that if Britain went off the gold standard it would be the end of all things. While we have gone quite a long way in our monetary system since then, I am confident that many changes will have to be made before we overpower the pagan hordes let loose in Europe to-day.
While I commend the minister for the steps he has already taken to pay as much of our war expenditure as possible out of taxes, I suggest to him that perhaps even a greater use might be made of the Bank of Canada. In fact, I believe we shall have to have some form of managed currency before this war is over, and I am not so sure but that that process has not already been started. Therefore, instead of thinking entirely in terms of money, let us not lose sight of the fact that so long as we have ample labour power plus land and the required materials, and so long as the sun shines and the rain falls from heaven, we must find ways and means to 14873-162
produce to our very utmost the weapons of war required, and that quickly. In other words, we must make our financial system fit into all the material things required to win out, such as food, guns, ships, tanks, aeroplanes, munitions and so forth, rather than continue to do what we have been doing in the past, making our financial system our first object of consideration; for it is true, Mr. Speaker, that to most of us nothing matters but the overthrow of this demon whose evident purpose now is the destruction of Great Britain and the other democracies.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has stated that during the present 'fiscal year Canadian shipments to Britain of munitions, raw materials and agricultural products will reach approximately one and a half billion dollars worth. While I am not at this time going to enter into a detailed discussion of how Great Britain will meet these commitments, might I suggest that we should prepare now by reducing further the tariffs we have placed against the entry of British goods into Canada. Canada, it is true, is straining every effort to produce the munitions of war which Britain so urgently requires, but we are buying back from Britain just as few goods as possible. In the past few years we have been keeping British goods out of this country to help Canadian manufacturers; but as Britain can pay us only in goods, should we now, in the light of what is taking place, continue to keep the door closed against goods from Great Britain?
Last year, in 1940, Canada purchased from Britain only $160,000,000 worth of goods, on which a duty of $16,500,000 was collected before the goods were allowed into this country. As has already been pointed out, Canada will ship to Great Britain this year over one billion dollars worth more of supplies than Britain will send to us. We are providing these supplies without cash payments, by a process known technically as the accumulation of sterling balances, the actual details of which have not yet for certain good reasons been made public. It is, however, well known to all who have given any study to such matters that if there is one thing more than another which has helped to contribute to the present world crisis, it is that practically every country prior to 1939 had built a tariff wall round itself, and for that policy both the United States and Canada must accept some responsibility. Selfishness and economic nationalism were largely responsible for a great deal of our difficulties before the war, and I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if we are really serious in hoping for a better world in the days to come when this war is over, we had better start now working on new plans for

The Budget-Mr. Reid

the dawn of that better day. Our outlook on life must be much broader and more humane and must include the people of other lands as well as our own. It is pointed out in holy writ that it is not good for man to dwell alone, and this injunction applies with equal force to the nations of the earth. In other words, let us remember if we can that the brotherhood of man envisions all peoples.
I have nothing but praise for the assistance that is being given to Britain by our friends and neighbours of the United States. Not only are they providing the much needed war materials and ships, but at the same time they are"saying to Britain under the lease-lend act: Do not worry about payment.
It was refreshing to hear not long ago the words of a United States senator, who said that the United States was prepared to supply Great Britain with everything they had in the United States, and that if the Germans interfered, the United States would blow the hell out of them. Strong language, Mr. Speaker, but I am of opinion that a little of that kind of language would not hurt in this country.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) some time ago paid tribute to that outstanding American Mr. Wendell Willkie, a tribute which I believe all Canadians heartily endorse. I cannot, however, help comparing Mr. Willkie's attitude towards the president and government of the United States since the last presidential election with that of the leader of the opposition and other members of his party in their criticism of our prime minister and members of the government since the last election. Mr. Willkie by his speeches and by his entire attitude of mind and purpose has done more, I believe, to help guide and unite public thought and opinion in the United States than has been the case with the opposing political parties in Canada, and I commend even at this late date to the leader of the opposition the example set by Mr. Willkie, who at a time when he might 'have spoken in a critical political way, nevertheless, realizing that the life of this country was in jeopardy, rose to the occasion and, sweeping aside all thoughts of political criticism, affirmed in those memorable words, "President Roosevelt is my president". This statement of Mr. Willkie showed that, although he had opposed Mr. Roosevelt during the election, 'he accepted the will of the people in the noblest sense of the word. I mention this not in any carping sense but simply because of the seriousness of war conditions to-day.
It may be true that our Prime Minister has no great flair for notoriety or glamour, but what other man in Canada to-day could hold the balance between this restless country with its diversified peoples as well as he does? What other man could so well maintain our 
position between Great Britain and the United States to the utmost advantage of all three?
I wish at this stage to sound a note of warning to the government regarding the farmers and farm conditions generally throughout the country. The farmers as a class are and have been more than eager to do their part fully in this crisis and to do everything in their power to help defeat Hitlerism. They have also been willing to share freely with the people of Britain what they grow and produce. They are, however, wondering about industry's part in this war and are seriously asking whether the government expects them to continue to produce the nation's food; at prices away below the actual cost of production whilst industry prospers. They are not objecting to industrial workers and others having plenteous and continuous employment at fair or better than living wages; but if the government is going to see to it that industrial wages are maintained at the year 1926 level, one cannot blame the farmer if he rebels or even leaves the farm on account of prevailing low farm prices and because no steps have been taken to protect him such as have been taken by the government respecting workers in industry. If the low farm prices, with the resultant distress accompanying such low prices, are ignored and the policy is continued whereby only the industrial workers in this country such as in shipyards, machine shops and war factories are assured of a decent living wage or standard of living, then I am afraid we are going to encourage a class discontent amongst our farmers which is not desirable, and Which might to some extent affect our all-out war effort. The farmers are, I think, fairly reasonable people, and when they ask for a reasonable price for their produce, comparable at least with that of 1926, I believe all will agree with me that they are not asking too much. We must expect sacrifices of some kind during this crisis, but no one group or class should be required to bear these alone.
The statement by the Minister of Finance that for the duration of the war no attempt will be made by the dominion government to reopen the question of the Sirois report will, I believe, be received with mixed feelings throughout the country. In my opinion one of the reasons for the failure of dominion-provincial conferences called to discuss amendments to the British North America Act is the great change which has taken place in our political set-up since 1867, and not to the fathers of confederation being greater intellects-great as they undoubtedly were- than the men of our own day, as some seem to think. In Canada to-day we have quite a number of political parties, and this fact tends, I believe, to influence discussions and

The Budget-Mr. Reid
255V
decisions at these conferences. I suggest that when future conferences of the provinces are called, the changed conditions compared with those of 1867 should not be overlooked, and more consideration should be given to possible representation from the various provinces invited to participate in such deliberations. However, I commend the Minister of Finance for the steps attempted as proposed in the budget to implement one of the chief, if not the chief recommendation in' the Sirois report, namely, income tax collections solely by the dominion government. In the light of the new income tax schedule in effect now, it is going to be rather difficult, I believe, for the various provinces not to agree to the proposals made by the minister; for, as it stands now, the onus or responsibility of further increased income tax payments from the Canadian people rests with each province. The dominion government has not nearly as good a case for entering the field of gasoline taxation as for invading the income tax field, when it is remembered that the responsibility for roads and road construction is taken care of by provincial governments. However, it is fully realized that money must be found for our war expenditures and commitments, and the fact that these are to be met as far as is possible out of taxation will be approved by the Canadian people generally. If the tax on gasoline is also the means of conserving much needed foreign exchange through a control of gasoline consumption, no great exception will be taken to the tax imposed of three cents a gallon.
Here may I say that I should have liked the minister to give the same assurance regarding the gasoline tax as he gave with regard to the income tax, namely, that it would be only for the duration of the war, because I am of opinion that once the dominion government have invaded this field, they may be inclined to stay in it.
This afternoon I listened to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party, when he dealt particularly with the ten per cent tax imposed on railway, steamship, motor bus and aeroplane fares. I differ a little from him in my criticism of this impost, because, first of all, I realize how large a sum of money the government has to find with which to pay our war commitments, and I am mindful also of the fact that no one could introduce any form of taxation to which some objection could not be raised. My criticism regarding the ten per cent tax on railway and other fares is along different lines. I am wondering whether the government gave any consideration to H873-1621
including among those taxable under this proposal those who travel by way of free passes. It may interest the house to know that the number of passes issued in Canada for travel on our railways has reached the enormous ratio of about one in every fifteen of our population. Here are the actual figures of the number of free railway passes as given in the report of the royal commission on railways and transportation, 1931, which figures are the only ones procurable. Just why the number of railway passes issued should be regarded as secret I am at a loss to understand, but I have been informed that they are so regarded by the board of transport commissioners, a body about which, by the wav, I shall have something to say later on.
The figures I quote are from the Duff commission report, and relate to 1930, the latest year for which I can get information, because, as I have already pointed out, the board of transport commissioners contend that these returns are secret. These are the
figures: *
Long service annual	passes	 130.895
Railway employees and	dependents 555,298
Other trip passes	 38,209
Trip passes for members of parliament and senators and their dependents	 11,078
Total	 744,480
This number has, I believe, been increased since 1930, although the passenger traffic on our railways has decreased since then by some 20,000,000. In 1930 the total number of passengers carried was not much below 40,000,000, while in 1938, the last year for which I have been able to get figures, approximately only 20,000,000 passengers were carried.
Here we have on the one hand a large group or class who not only can travel free on our railways, but are also going to be exempt from the payment of this ten per cent tax, whilst on the other hand all those who pay for their transportation will be called upon for a further ten per cent. This is class legislation of a nature which to my mind is most unfair. No great objection was made when the ten per cent was placed on the costs of berths; for there, it was assumed that those who bought berths on the train were able to pay a tax of some kind. But when you come to the question of a ten per cent tax which is confined solely to purchased transportation, the principle is entirely different. Let us see what takes place with those who have to pay their fare on a journey from, say, Ottawa to Vancouver. On a round-trip fare the railway cost is $128 for the standard coach, which amount the ten per cent tax increases by S12.80. Or take the case of our
The Budget-Mr. Reid

enlisted soldiers who may wish to travel home. Is the government going to tax our fighting men ten per cent in addition to the cost of their fares, while certain privileged groups or classes are exempt from the payment of this tax and also travel free of charge? Either the government should tax everyone who travels on trains, boats, buses or aeroplanes, or it should rescind this tax entirely. Class legislation of this kind will tend only to create friction. It is not the tax alone which will be objected to, but the fact that thousands of others, who could pay, are exempt. I trust that the minister will take this matter under consideration before the budget finally passes.
The question of free railway passes is a matter apart from this, but something to which serious attention should be given. Grave abuses have grown up under this system. I am not unreservedly blaming those who make use of free railway travelling privileges, human nature being what it is. Even for members of parliament and members of the senate, the practice in use in Great Britain has much to commend it. In passing, I would call the attention of the government to the recommendation on this matter which is to be found on page 46 of the Duff commission report. It is there suggested that the powers vested in the board of transportation commissioners as to the issuance of passes be reviewed. This has not, so far as I know, been done.
There is one other matter of importance to which I should like to refer at this time. It is one which I brought up last year but about which nothing so far has been done; that is, the question of a high-powered short-wave radio station for Canada. We in this country can tune in on short-wave radio sets and hear what is going on in almost every other country in the world to-day, but we can only listen to what comes over the air; we cannot speak or answer back to people in other lands, which we could do but for the fact that Canada, almost alone among the countries of the world, has no short-wave radio station powerful enough for the purpose.
I am going to mention only some of the opportunities and advantages which Canada is missing owing to our not having such a station in use to-day. First, there is the fact that Canada is one of the great trading nations of the world, being fifth or sixth among the nations in the matter of total trade. Canada, again, has a perpetual and everlasting asset to sell, namely, that of our wonderful scenic beauty, particularly that of British Columbia. Apart from a few trade commissioners and some newspaper advertisements in foreign newspapers and magazines, we refuse to make

use of the modern means of telling the outside world the good things we have in abundance in Canada. It would almost appear as if we were afraid the other countries might get to know of these things; and, as I have already stated, we listen to all outside countries speaking to us but refuse to answer or even to speak to them.
There is no denying the fact that people in other lands, particularly in the countries of north and south America, would appreciate something direct from the great Dominion of Canada. In fact, they are wondering what is wrong with us that they do not hear direct over the air from and about Canada. Consider also the great help we could render Great Britain during these serious times if Canada could only speak direct to the conquered countries of Europe, yes, and even perhaps to the people of Germany as well. I wonder just when we are going to wake up to the fact that the radio is also one of the most powerful and effective means of terror propaganda which is being used by the Germans to-day and which we in Canada make no attempt to circumvent. In this regard, let me read to the house what one who knows has to say about it. I quote from an article which appeared in the Vancouver Sun of April 29 of this year under the heading "Expert Warns of 'German Radio Terror'":
The radio propaganda in Germany is "a menace and a terror" that has taken the place of the artillery barrage and with more effectiveness than any artillery in the last war.
Charles A. Siepmann, formerly with the British Broadcasting Corporation, now radio adviser to Harvard university, told members of the Vancouver Canadian club on Monday that there is danger that something of the kind may work just as ruinously in Canada and the United States.
The German radio propaganda has been "skilful beyond description" and at present it is aimed at the people of the United States through voices that carry the pronunciations and idioms of every section of the country.
He described the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as "a brave experiment" in trying to put public service alongside a privately operated system of commercial broadcasting.
The great challenge to the CBC is that it is the one great integrating force for building a real sense of Canadian unity-for making the far-flung parts of the country known to each other.
To my mind, it is dangerous for us to sit idly by and do nothing to keep the people in all countries, including Germany itself, informed on matters which are deemed desirable; and, as everyone knows, we cannot prevent anyone in this country, if he so desires, from listening in to foreign broadcasts. In view, further, of the severe bombing taking place in Britain, Canada should construct this short-wave station right away and

The Budget-Mr. Fraser (Peterborough)
so have in this country a powerful radio station in reserve and in case of severe damage to the British Broadcasting Corporation, which might yet be put out of business for a time at least. How wonderful also if Canada could do as Australia is able to do and has been doing by speaking direct to our fighting men either in Great Britain or elsewhere!
Before I leave this part of my remarks I want, as seriously as I can, to warn both the government and the country that if Canada does not quickly avail herself of a powerful short-wave radio station, it may be, when we decide to have one, that it will be found we cannot do so. My information is that there are only a number of channels, or frequencies as they are called, available in the air, and that these are being taken up by other countries. In other words, radio lines in the atmosphere are not unlimited. There are only a definite number available, and soon- very soon-there will be none left. Canada cannot afford to wait much longer, and therefore I urge the government to make haste now and so secure for the Canadian people one of the still available channels of air, before it is too late. Are we, for the sake of half a million dollars, going to run the risk of losing out and so make Canada inferior to, or perhaps dependent upon, other nations for all time to come?
May I also at this time bring to the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Howe) the position of the people in British Columbia with regard to radio under the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. There have been provided by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in the maritimes, in Ontario, in Quebec and also for the prairie provinces, radio stations of fifty kilowatts or 50,000 watts. These are of such a power that no great difficulties are being experienced, I believe, by the people using radios in those provinces. In British Columbia the one station provided under the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is located in Vancouver. This station, however, is only of a power of five kilowatts or 5.000 watts, just one-tenth of the power of each of the other stations mentioned. The result is that many people in British Columbia, especially those in the interior, get no radio service whatsoever from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation station in Vancouver, and unless better service is provided it is suggested that the collecting of a S2.50 tax from those without such service be delayed until this state of affairs is rectified. We in British Columbia are surely entitled to some better consideration than has been given us, especially When it is
realized that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation station for the entire province at Vancouver is only one-tenth as powerful as that provided in the other provinces.
Just a word or two in closing. The budget introduced by the Minister of Finance will, I believe, bring home to the Canadian people some realization of what Canada is doing in connection with our war effort. It is my firm belief that our people will respond willingly to the demands made upon them. To everyone who loves and values the right of the individual to have some say over his own life, there can be only one answer to the menace of Hitlerism. To any who may still have any doubts, I would ask them to inquire of the people in the countries overrun by the German hordes what they think now of the gestapo methods of government. The latest news from Germany, whereby it was decreed that some 80,000 of their own people should be put to death, whose only crime against the state was that they had grown old or were infirm, will, I trust, arouse our own people to a grave sense of the danger of not fully realizing the type of enemy we have to combat. The treatment meted out to these people is an example of what Great Britain, Canada and the other democracies may expect should Hitlerism prevail, and we in Canada will indeed be fortunate if no greater sacrifices are required from us than those that have been requested in the present budget.

The heading is:
In accordance with memorandum series D No. 50 TD & R 18 second revision, the publications listed by titles hereunder are ruled to be exempt from the payment of the war exchange tax. . . .
These are issued every day or so; I will send one over to the minister. We have a war on at the present time, and I feel that it would be a great deal better to make these magazines pay that tax and use the money collected to reduce the national defence tax on our workmen. Thousands of magazines are coming in absolutely free.
I would suggest also that exemptions be allowed on income tax for children twenty-one years of age and over, at present attending school. As soon as children become twenty-one years old, the $400 exemption is removed. Many people have girls who are away at school or college, and their expenses amount to a great deal more than $400. I
2562	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Fraser (Peterborough)
know; I have one myself, and many others? have spoken to me about this matter. I would suggest that the exemption be allowed for girls only while they are at school, because a boy can get out during the summer holidays and make a few dollars for himself. I am sure many hon. members had to do that, as I did when I went to school, and I believe we were a great deal the better for it.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) mentioned the matter of railway passes. I should like to quote from an editorial in this regard:
Word from Ottawa indicates that holders of passes will not have to pay the new dominion taxes on railway fares and theatre tickets. The, explanation is that the new order says the tax must be paid "by every purchaser of transportation," and the individual with a pass does not purchase transportation.
In theatres the tax is collected on the receipts, and those who have passes are not contributing anything to those receipts. And yet after having read the explanation one is inclined to ask that plain question: "Why are any exceptions made?" We are all in this thing together; we are all paying together, and we doubt if those who possess passes for transportation or anything else would ask to be excused while others are putting up their assessment.
The only exception I would make is to exempt the soldiers from paying a tax on their fares. A soldier coming home to Peterborough from Halifax must pay $23, whereas excursions have been run for $20 and some odd cents, giving the civilian a preference over the soldier.
The hon. member for New Westminster referred to the use of short-wave radio by the Germans as a weapon of war. This is perfectly true, and I mentioned this fact some months ago in this house. I would advise hon. members to read the speech made in the British House of Commons by Captain Leonard Plugge who is considered to be one of the best radio experts in the British empire.
I have made a few suggestions and I am going to make a few more. The Minister of Finance is looking for more money, and as much as possible we should try to pay our way as we go along. I suggest that a tax be put on meals served in restaurants or hotels and costing one dollar or more. If anyone can pay a dollar for a meal he can certainly afford an extra five or ten cents. This would bring in considerable revenue to the dominion. I think the suggestion put forward this afternoon by my leader (Mr. Hanson) was very good. At the present time the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is bonusing the growing of rye and other coarse grains in the west. I think the Minister of Finance should tax rye, only the wet kind, and all other hard liquors. I am sure that this would be a popular tax.

The gasoline tax of three cents a gallon is quite heavy when considered along with the provincial tax of eight cents a gallon. I do not think this tax will discourage tourists coming from the United States if the dominion will place at all ports of entry signs stating that the Canadian gallon is one-fifth larger than the United States gallon. When that is taken into consideration, along with the premium paid on the United States dollar, it will be found that a tourist from the United States is not paying a great deal more for his gasoline.
In conclusion, I should like to repeat what I said in this house some weeks ago. The Minister of Finance should see that every person receiving from this government a wage, indemnity or pension of over $3,000 should be compelled to take at least ten per cent in war savings certificates, non-transferable and not to be redeemed for at least seven years. This must be done if this government wish to show the people that they practise what they preach.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in making my first contribution in this house, may I say that I considered my first duty on coming to this house one year ago was to assist the government in every way by voting supply to carry on the war effort of Canada. I felt that it was my further duty to assist in passing the implementing legislation required to give this government the broad powers which all governments must have in times of war. I felt that all this could best be accomplished by refraining from making unnecessary speeches. Having confidence in this government and recognizing its ability, energy and zeal, I did not think it was necessary to enlarge upon these facts by much speaking. However, after listening to many of the speakers from various groups in the opposition, as well on this side of the house, I felt that this was the time for me to express myself on behalf of a goodly number of people in Saskatchewan and express a few

The Budget-Mr. Gregory
ideas Which may not have been expressed up to the present or which may not be in agreement with others expressed already.
Since this session was convened, a dominion-provincial conference was held to discuss the implementing of the recommendations of the report of the Sirois commission. As we all know, this conference was torpedoed. Something over two years ago when the legislative assembly of Saskatchewan met following the presentation of the Saskatchewan brief to the then Rowell commission, I had this to say in the new legislative assembly:
That a new bill of rights had been written for Saskatchewan and that the dawn of a better day was breaking if this brief was implemented in legislation.
I should like to point out that the western provinces were settled in a different manner from that in which the older provinces of Canada were. There were no forests to be cleared and there were comparatively few swamps to be drained. The land in the west was ready for the plough, and the population of the west was obtained by a national policy of advertising to the world that free homesteads and cheap land were available to those who wished them. The result was a tide of land-hungry immigrants which swept across Canada in increasing volume every year, until a peak of over half a million new settlers was reached in 1912-13.
The railroads followed in the wake of the settlers, rather than the settlers following in the wake of the railways. Villages, towns and cities sprang up, and municipal governments, rural and urban school districts and all other services incidental to modern life were thrust upon the new settlers. City improvements, schools, telephone lines, roads and bridges were constructed in a hurry. A great burden was placed upon the two new provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta when they were formed in 1905. Legislative buildings had to be built and legal machinery provided. Court houses, land title offices, highways, bridges, gaols, mental hospitals, homes for the aged, and trunk telephone lines sprang up throughout the province like mushrooms. This, of necessity, created a heavy capital bonded debt. Since it was a new and untried country, high rates of interest were demanded on its bond issues. The price thus paid to create a modern civilized country out of western Canada was a heavy one. All our various institutions had thrust upon them within the space of a decade or two a task which was spread over at least three generations of our older provinces. Provincial government, municipal government, urban and rural, and school districts all carry an immense load of bonded debt in my province.
There is, however, another phase of economic life from which western Canada has suffered throughout its whole history.
I am speaking, Mr. Speaker, from a residence of forty-four years in western Canada and from an experience of thirty-six years spent in the city in which I now reside, the city of North Battleford. I think then, sir, I understand the problems of my province.
I say that there is another phase of economic life from which western Canada has suffered throughout its whole history.
I refer to the tariff, that hackneyed, outworn and time-honoured word, the tariff. This has been an increasing burden upon western Canada as the years have gone by. To the consumer it has meant a burden upon everything he buys. It has been estimated by the late Hon. Norman Rogers, who prepared for the Duncan commission that famous brief on the incidence of the tariff burden on the various provinces, that Saskatchewan annually was contributing $29,000,000 by way of tariff burden. Then, as regards the producer to the extent that the tariff operates as a prohibition against the purchase of foreign goods, just to that extent does the tariff act as a restriction on the sales of the producer's goods in those foreign countries to which those goods should be sold.
There is a further burden placed upon the western Canadian. There was a period within the memory of all present in this house when the tariff of Canada was the chief, almost the sole revenue of the dominion. As tariffs were raised by different governments, the revenues from this source diminished relatively, due to the higher tariffs acting as a prohibition against the importation of foreign goods.
Resort was then had to other forms of taxation-direct taxation, income tax, the sales tax, which has been increased from time to time, excise taxes on sugar, tobacco and various other items. Therefore western Canadians are not only penalized by paying high tariff penalties, but are again penalized by all these various forms of direct taxation.
For a moment let us consider the economic flow of wealth in Canada which has persisted for at least the last fifty years. I can remember when the maritime provinces had their own banks, trust companies, mortgage companies, insurance companies, and their own factory industry. I ask you, sir, where are those institutions to-day? Those
The Budget

Mr. Gregory

which have survived have largely moved to the central provinces, and by the central provinces I refer, of course, to Ontario and Quebec; or they have been absorbed by other institutions whose head offices are in the central provinces.
What has been the direction of economic flow of wealth so far as the west is concerned? For over forty years to my own personal knowledge, western Canada has produced prodigious wealth from the lands, the mines and the forests. Where is that wealth to-day? Certainly not in western Canada. Every cent of interest paid in that period of time to the banks, mortgage companies and land companies of all kinds has gone to the central provinces. Every insurance premium, whether it be fire, life, accident, sickness or casualty, has gone to the central provinces, and vast sums of our purchasing power have gone to the industries of the central provinces, mostly to the province of Ontario and the city of Montreal. The wealth of the west has made big banks out of small banks in the central provinces. It has made big insurance companies, big trust companies, big mortgage companies out of small ones in the central provinces. It has made big factories out of small factories in the central provinces, and again may I say, Mr. Speaker, that I am quite well aware of the size of the factories of Ontario when I left this province^where I was born and raised. I remember the size of the Massey-Harris company, Cockshutt Plow and all the rest of them in Ontario, and I am therefore speaking from first hand knowledge when I say that during the last forty years the wealth of the west has made big industries out of small industries in this province. It has created work in this province to increase capital outlay. It has created jobs by the hundreds of thousands to man the increased machines in the expanding industries in the central provinces.
The climax of my argument is this, that the wealth of western Canada has made small incomes in the central provinces large incomes, and small accumulations of wealth, large fortunes, and it is from these large incomes that provincial income tax is paid to Ontario and from these large fortunes that succession duties are paid to Ontario. My argument is that western Canada, which largely made it possible for these large income taxes and succession duties to be paid, has an equitable interest in these revenues which it has largely created, that these enormous revenues do not wholly belong to the province of Ontario by right, and that therefore these revenues should be collected solely by the federal government 
in trust for all the people of Canada, to be distributed back to the people on a per capita basis.
I have tried to show that all the various institutions of western Canada are heavily burdened by debt, that the original pioneer who made that country is heavily burdened by debt, that through the very nature and development of this country that had to be. Moreover I have tried to show that the development of western Canada has made a vast contribution to the wealth and welfare of the rest of Canada. It is, therefore, justified in asking for a recognition of its just claims under confederation. The rejection of even a discussion of the Sirois commission's recommendations was a death-blow to Saskatchewan, which cannot carry on under the present set-up. The demands of each institution of government, federal, provincial, municipal and school district, upon the individual taxpayer, already heavily indebted, are beyond human ability to meet. These demands cannot be met.
There remains but one avenue of escape, and that is for us in Saskatchewan to live more within the resources of the province. This would mean less fruit and fish and lumber from British Columbia, less coal from Alberta, and less of manufactured goods from Ontario. This is intended to be neither an expressed nor an implied threat of reprisals. It is simply a plain statement of fact arising from the impossible position in which my province finds itself. I place myself beside Premier Bracken of Manitoba and Premier Patterson of my own province of Saskatchewan in condemning the break-up of this conference and in urging, yes pleading, that there be a future and further consideration of these problems.
May I say one word with respect to a subject which likewise has been worn threadbare in this house and of which most hon. members are tired of hearing the name; I refer to the question of wheat. In the brief reference I have to make to the farming community in western Canada, let me say that no class in the country has suffered as has the western wheat grower. During the last war he was encouraged by the government of the day to grow more wheat as a national duty. He therefore bought more land at inflated prices. He bought large units of machinery, power-drawn, in order to meet the inflated wages of the day. He burdened himself with debt at high rates of interest. He met a national emergency as it was presented to him at that particular time. Then followed the collapse of 1921. Recovery set in some four years later, followed again by

The Budget-Mr. Gregory
the collapse of 1929, which meant ruination to the farmer so far as prices are concerned. For the farmer in my country, every year since 1929 has been a ruinous year. Added to the deflation of the world crisis, drought has visited every part of western Canada intermittently since that time. Farmers have been selling below cost of production, when they had anything to sell, each year since 1929. In addition to the living which the farmer did not obtain, there is depreciation to consider, and interest on debts which have been piling up with no hope of better times. Secondary industry in Canada is pretty well assured against loss. Consideration has been given to wages of labour. With each of these, Mr. Speaker, I have no quarrel. The farmer is bearing his burden nobly and patriotically, and is prepared to carry his share of the load, but he cannot help thinking that in contributing his share of the national war effort he should be allowed at least to live.
I quite realize that there can be no satisfactory solution of the wheat problem while Hitler's armies are occupying the countries with which we normally trade. I would go further and say that there can be no satisfactory solution of the wheat question so long as narrow nationalism prevails in the countries of Europe. As you are aware, sir, fear of war created in the last twenty years these policies which we call narrow nationalism, and until war ceases and the fear of war vanishes from the earth there will be no free interchange of products amongst the countries of the world, each producing what it is best fitted to produce, selling the surpluses in foreign markets, and purchasing in exchange from foreign markets what each requires. That time has not yet arrived. What shall we do in the meantime? I assume that there is only one answer to that question. We must make a compromise agreement with respect to this wheat problem.
The other day we had a compromise agreement brought down for the consideration of this house. I realize that any cabinet decision upon a problem of this kind must be a compromise decision. There are in Canada many provinces and many interests, each presenting its viewpoint and each exerting its influence upon the national federal cabinet, and all decisions on questions of this kind by the government of the day must, therefore, be in the nature of a compromise. We in the west realize that the population of Canada largely lies east of the great lakes. We realize that the wealth and the organization and, therefore, the influence lie east of the great lakes, and that whatever treatment the west receives is with the consent of the east. We are prepared even to concede at times
that the east has viewed western problems with that broad outlook of the welfare of Canada as a whole. We wish to express our appreciation of that fact. But in all future considerations of the wheat problem-and I have no intention of raising any of the issues which have been fought and decided-may I ask our eastern friends to remember that western wheat is woven into the warp and the woof of the industrial, financial and commercial fabric of Canada, and because of that fact may I urge that this problem be approached in succeeding years by hon. members from the east with a broad charity and, I trust, a broader knowledge of the problems which the western wheat grower has been enduring ever since the collapse of 1929.
Since coming down to this house I have tried to learn something with regard to the financial religion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley). I was pleased to read the following statement in a speech which he delivered at Timmins on Labour day, 1940:
We have learned, the world has learned, that sound monetary management in our modern industrial society requires flexibility and judgment in national monetary policies.
In that statement, I wholly concur. It would appear to me that the minister is following the good example of the previous Minister of Finance, who, I believe, in that capacity made his name as a great statesman and a great Canadian. I refer to the Hon. Charles A. Dunning. May I quote one or two sentences from a speech delivered by Mr. Dunning in this house on March 9, 1938, as recorded in the Regina Leader-Post:
The Bank of Canada did regulate currency and credit with the single purpose of promoting the best interests of the country. It was following an easy money policy, expanding the currency base and the volume of credit at a rate it believed to be in the best interests of the nation.
By the purchase and sale of securities and by the use of the discount rate, the bank regulated the volume of credit in circulation. Purchase of securities increased bank deposits and credit; sale reduced them. A higher discount rate curtailed business expansion. A lower rate fostered expansion.
Just one more sentence:
We are not now on the gold standard. We are not subject to its deflationary or other influence. For better or for worse we are now on a managed paper currency, just as the United Kingdom. The value of Canadian currency was determined, not by gold but by the factors operating on a managed currency, chiefly demand and supply. The Bank of Canada controlled the operations of the chartered banks by purchase and sale of securities. . . .
And so forth. That is all I will read from that speech. I have also been gratified since coming to this house to hear later statements
The Budget-Mr. Gregory

from the Minister of Finance that credit has been expanded as rapidly as production and that there is at the present time in Canada sufficient credit to take care of production. Again, I wish to concur heartily in that statement read. My conception of a credit structure is one designed to meet all contingencies of production, one designed for the welfare of our citizens, and not managed and controlled for the welfare and profits of stockholders, a currency and credit structure so balanced that distribution may be the partner of production, and the effect of which will be that price levels of both commodities and labour will be kept on an even keel. I should like to feel that we have relegated to the dungeons of past barbarities those cruel instruments of torture of private banking methods which have been used so effectively in the past in creating inflation of price levels, followed by inhuman deflation of values, by which the greed of a few sucked in the assets of the many.
We have now in the Bank of Canada the necessary instrument to control the financial economy of our nation, and the people of Canada will hold this government and successive governments strictly to account for the proper use of this instrument.
If I may, for a few minutes, I should like now to refer to another phase of life in western Canada. We have another problem in my province of Saskatchewan, and, to some extent, in the whole of western Canada. I refer to the subversive propaganda which has been taught to the people from the public platform by those posing as leaders of the people, in some instances by those who should be leaders of the people in every sense of the word. I do not know who is financing the tours of some of these public speakers, but some of these meetings are held under auspices which, to say the least, are not outstanding in their zeal to assist in the war effort of Canada.
My province has a population of whom nearly 50 per cent are foreign born or are the offspring of foreign bom, and I think it is reasonable to assume that these people cannot be expected to have the same veneration for those things which we call British as those born of British stock, British traditions and British institutions, so dearly and so slowly won and fought for down through the ages. It should surely then, Mr. Speaker, be the duty of those coming from British stock to inculcate into the foreign bom the value of the heritage which became theirs in a British land-freedom, democracy, the right to choose and to live the chosen life within the law. It should be the duty of all public speakers at this particular time to inculcate two things and to insist upon these two things. The
[Mr. Greeory.l
first is the promotion of the war effort of Canada, to encourage the people to think in terms of the seriousness of the effects of this war upon Canadian life; and the second is to encourage the people to save, to give, to pay, to assist in the financing of this war. It should be stressed on all public occasions that, unless we win the war, democracy, freedom and our way of life are all gone, and that all should drop petty differences in the greater and more important task of defeating Hitler and crushing him and all for which he stands.
What do I find as I follow these speeches through Saskatchewan, Alberta, some in British Columbia and even in Ontario? I find that fear is being instilled into the minds of every audience-fear that the government has enslaved the people; fear that the government is domineering over the people instead of being the servant of the people; fear that the defence of Canada regulations have destroyed democracy and the rights and liberties of the people; fear that liberties lost in war time may not be regained in peace time. May I say right here, sir, that these opinions are not the beliefs and opinions of my constituents or of the people of Saskatchewan as a whole, and I believe I know the views of the people of Saskatchewan. I believe I know the opinions and the beliefs of the people of that province. I have seen most of them come into that province; I have seen nearly every mile of railway built in that country, and I think I am in a position to judge properly what the viewpoints and opinions of these people are.
I have noticed all through life, yes, through a fairly long life, that it does not require [DOT] courage or capacity to appeal to fear and prejudice and ignorance of masses of people and to arouse and disturb their minds with vague doubts. That is the simplest thing in the world. I have seen throughout my whole life demagogues do this on public platforms without possessing either balance or brillance, and set a peaceful people aflame with passion and prejudice. For any public speaker to suggest that the people are disturbed and bewildered and are filled with fear over the actions of this government or the operations of the defence of Canada regulations is only to suggest, to my mind, that if there be a shred of truth in that statement, then this disturbance or bewilderment or fear was not in the minds of these audiences until the speaker placed it there.
Parliaments are elected by the people of Canada, just as in England parliaments are elected by the people. That is democracy. Governments are selected from the majority party in the people's parliament. That is democracy. Laws are passed by majorities

The Budget-Mr. Gregory
in parliament. That is democracy. The defence of Canada regulations are based upon the War Measures Act; that act was passed by this parliament. Those regulations are amended each year by a committee of the house and then presented to the house for further consideration. This parliament does the same as every other parliament in the British domains; in times of war this parliament proposes to give the government of the day very broad powers in order to carry on the war effort of the country.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police are charged with the responsibility of investigating and tracking down disloyal activities, and surely no one will suggest that this force has not the respect and cofidenee of all Canadians. We in the west respected and admired and placed our confidence in this force for nearly two generations before the rest of Canada knew anything about the old Northwest Mounted Police. Reports, of all investigations, are made by this force to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), and only on the authority of the minister does an internment take place. The internee then has the right to be heard before a tribunal, and who would suggest that the principles of British justice are violated in any respect in all the operations under the defence of Canada regulations?
Talking about governments tending to become our masters when they should be our servants is just a play upon words, just a hollow play upon words. I was surprised to hear the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) with his knowledge of law and constitutional development and of the Anglo-Saxon struggle for responsible government, express his sympathy with a statement made in this house to the effect that the government had become the masters of the people. Of course the government is the government. We expect it to be the government, the executive of the people's legislative assembly to carry out the powers granted it under the statutes passed by the people's parliament. In that regard it is the servant of the people, through the people's representatives. But at the same time we expect it to be the government of the people. When the time comes that the people of this country think this government is not sufficiently carrying out their wishes,-shall I say as their servant?- when that time comes all that the people of this country have to do is to elect another parliament of a different complexion, and there will soon be a change in the personnel of that government. Those are the checks, and those are the safeguards under which we operate in the British domains.
I have spoken longer than I intended, but there are a few other things I wish to say this evening, seeing it is the first time I have had the pleasure of speaking in this larger legislative assembly. I have here reports of a great many public meetings held throughout Canada. I shall refer this evening to only about four of them. I have the report of a meeting held in the city of Oshawa from the Toronto Star of December 9, last. The heading of the article is, "We behave like a bunch of cowards." I shall quote just an odd sentence or two:
We people in Canada, since those defence of Canada regulations were passed, have behaved like a bunch of cowards. We have felt afraid we would get into trouble if we raised our voice against them. . . .
At this meeting a resolution was passed in which it was stated:
We express it as our emphatic opinion that the defence of Canada regulations must be amended so as to guarantee the fullest freedom of speech, press and organization. . . .
We sometimes see puzzled expressions on people's faces when we speak of democracy. We use the word so glibly. What does it mean? . . .
The defence of Canada regulations . . . have destroyed the bulwarks of our freedom. We must get our freedom back. . . .
Then, from a meeting held in the town of Melville, Saskatchewan, I quote briefly:
In a democratic country the government . . . should be the servant of the people and not the master of the people as it had become in Canada.
(The speaker) indicated the people of Canada were asleep as they seemed to be ignorant of the loss of civil liberties under the defence of Canada regulations.

A meeting was held in Winnipeg, in the dining room of the Hudson's Bay store at which Professor Lower of the United college was chairman, and this opinion was expressed, fear that civil liberties lost in war time might not be regained in peace time. After the speech was delivered, the chairman commented that he would have nothing to do with any "hysterical movement." There is no advance to be made along such lines. Let me add that with these remarks I wholly agree.
I have several reports of meetings here, and I should like to crave another ten minutes. I shall put on record just one or two opinions from people who are capable of expressing a clear opinion as to what they think of this class of propaganda that
The Budget-Mr. Gregory

is going on throughout the length and breadth of Canada. The council of the Montreal board of trade appointed a committee for the purpose of making a thorough study of the defence of Canada regulations. I have before me their findings in full, but I shall quote only a sentence or two from a letter which the president sent out with copies of the full report:
The attached report has convinced the council of the board that no one can say with reason that these regulations do not conform with the principles of British justice, therefore no loyal citizen has anything to fear as a result of their enforcement. In fact it is the considered opinion of the council that the carrying out of these regulations, in their present form, is of the greatest importance in the protection of our Canadian homes, institutions and industrial activities.
It is strongly felt by the council that no Canadian can afford to be casual in this time of great danger and that any kind of propaganda or public statements that tend to weaken this instrument of protection should not he allowed to go unchallenged.
I should like now to refer to one or two other opinions expressed by some of our newspapers with respect to certain speeches.
